micro.label: Microhistory / everyday life
micro.description: Italian microstoria reconstructs relations and tests categories through close inquiry; German Alltagsgeschichte studies everyday practices and power. Neither is defined by small places alone, and their intellectual exchanges do not erase their differences.
micro.representative_figures_and_works: Carlo Ginzburg, The Cheese and the Worms (1976); Giovanni Levi; Alf Lüdtke. Natalie Zemon Davis: The Return of Martin Guerre (1983); Martin Broszat et al.: Bayern in der NS-Zeit (1977–83).

representative_people.context: Reconstructs Menocchio’s reading through inquisitorial records; later argues that narrative construction can coexist with evidentiary claims.
representative_people.works: The Cheese and the Worms (Italian 1976); “Microhistory: Two or Three Things That I Know about It” (1993)

representative_people.context: Reconstructs social relations and individual strategies at close range; Ginzburg’s account stresses their relation to wider contexts. His own methodological essays examine choices within conflicting norms and question fixed cultural contexts in interpretive history.
representative_people.works: Inheriting Power: The Story of an Exorcist (English 1988); I pericoli del geertzismo (1985); Les usages de la biographie (1989)

representative_people.context: Alltagsgeschichte researcher examining workers’ everyday practices, criticizing some structural priorities and drawing on Mann’s power networks.
representative_people.works: “Polymorphous Synchrony: German Industrial Workers and the Politics of Everyday Life” (1993)

representative_people.context: Examines occupational classification in Turin; Ginzburg identifies her relational reconstruction alongside Levi’s.
Microanalytical interlocutor whose formulation about exceptional evidence informs Ginzburg’s account of comparison.
representative_people.works: “Micro-analisi e storia sociale” (1977), discussed by Ginzburg (1993)

representative_people.context: Engages anthropology critically and collaboratively, including a working group with Lüdtke, Sabean and others.
representative_people.works: “Missionaries in the Row Boat”? (1987); with David Sabean, eds., Interest and Emotion (1984)

representative_people.context: Retrospective methodological interlocutor: Ginzburg praises his treatment of historical scale while explicitly denying known influence on microhistory’s emergence.
representative_people.works: History: The Last Things before the Last (1969), discussed by Ginzburg (1993), pp. 26–27

representative_people.context: An edited EHESS collection investigates changes of observational scale and generalization; it neither equates all small studies with microstoria nor makes small intrinsically superior. His own scale essay treats changed observation as changing the object and relationships available for analysis.
representative_people.works: Jeux d’échelles (editor, 1996); Micro-analyse et construction du social (1996)

representative_people.context: A critic of Alltagsgeschichte’s conceptual and explanatory claims who also acknowledges its cultural and experiential contributions.
representative_people.works: Alltagsgeschichte: Königsweg zu neuen Ufern oder Irrgarten der Illusionen? (1980s versions)

representative_people.context: Mexican local historian combining archives, conversations and lived experience for a local readership. This microhistoria is a distinct project, not a presumed branch of Italian microstoria.
representative_people.works: Pueblo en vilo (1968; revised edition consulted, 1979)

representative_people.context: González credits her corrections, proposed changes and preparation of the manuscript; the credited collaboration exceeds typing.
representative_people.works: Editorial collaboration on Pueblo en vilo, acknowledged in its preface

representative_people.context: Her preserved correspondence, association papers and long series of household accounts supplied González’s local history.
representative_people.works: Private archive and household expense notebooks used in Pueblo en vilo

representative_people.context: The Return of Martin Guerre (French 1982, the year of the film; English 1983) treats a village imposture. In ‘On the Lame’ (1988) she described her reconstruction from Coras, Le Sueur and the Parlement registers as a conjectural argument, and in 1997 she called her route ‘microhistory (or what I called ethnography) via film’. Finlay’s 1988 critique of its ‘invention’ and her reply are both recorded. Her cultural and women’s-history contexts remain.
representative_people.works: Le Retour de Martin Guerre (1982) and The Return of Martin Guerre (1983); “On the Lame” (AHR Forum, 1988)

representative_people.context: Led the Institut für Zeitgeschichte’s Bayern in der NS-Zeit project, a founding programme for the history of everyday life under National Socialism. His structuralist interpretation of the regime is a separate context.
representative_people.works: Bayern in der NS-Zeit (1977–1983), ed. with others

representative_people.context: Charges an ‘excess of invention’ in Davis’s portrait of Bertrande de Rols and insists on ‘the sovereignty of the sources’, while praising her portrait of peasant life; Davis replied in the same AHR Forum.

strands.title: Italian microstoria
strands.focus: A varied research programme connecting intensive cases to larger questions; cultural and social-relational inquiries overlap.

strands.title: Alltagsgeschichte
strands.focus: Lüdtke studies workers’ situated practices and power, using Mann as well as questioning structural priorities.
strands.works: “Polymorphous Synchrony” (1993); The History of Everyday Life (English 1995)

strands.title: Social relations and changing categories
strands.focus: Close reconstruction examines how relations and classifications are made through action.
strands.works: Levi, Inheriting Power; Cerutti, La Ville et les métiers

strands.title: Exceptional evidence and historical inference
strands.focus: An unusual case can expose assumptions without statistically representing a population.

strands.title: History and anthropology in working exchange
strands.focus: Critical engagement with Cohn and collaborative research complicate a one-way borrowing model.

strands.title: Moving between historical scales
strands.focus: Results at one scale cannot simply be transferred to another; retrospective affinity is distinguished from transmission.

strands.title: Everyday history, concepts and explanation
strands.focus: Wehler values the recovery of culture and experience but disputes claims to a replacement explanatory framework. Lüdtke challenges the reduction of everyday history to an illustrative supplement, while accepting some criticism of romanticization and insisting on reconstructing connections between traces. Both positions are internally qualified.

strands.title: Testing context through close interpretation
strands.focus: Levi argues that small episodes should revise the explanatory context, criticizing Darnton’s assumed cultural patterns while distinguishing Geertz’s accomplishments from mechanical applications.
strands.works: I pericoli del geertzismo (1985; Portuguese translation 1999)

strands.title: Choices within conflicting norms
strands.focus: Levi’s biography essay examines limited room for action and the formation of groups within contradictory normative systems; his disagreement with Bourdieu is one of emphasis.

strands.title: Varying scale changes the object of inquiry
strands.focus: Revel distinguishes changes of analytical scale from merely magnifying an unchanged object; no scale has an automatic privilege. Relational inquiry makes collective formation a problem to explain.
strands.works: Micro-analyse et construction du social (1996), sections 3–4

strands.title: Mexican microhistoria and local readership
strands.focus: González explains local events alongside regional and national pressures, combining documentary records, informal conversations and personal recollection. His claims to typicality and his treatment of uncorroborated memory are methodological choices open to criticism.

strands.title: Archives, informants and editorial collaboration
strands.focus: González’s preface credits Josefina’s archive, his father’s recollections, other informants and Armida’s revisions. These contributions make the local history a collaborative production despite its single-author title page.

strands.title: Reconstruction, invention and the sovereignty of sources
strands.focus: In ‘On the Lame’ (1988) Davis described her reconstruction of a village imposture from legal, notarial and printed records as conjectural, citing Ginzburg’s evidential paradigm; Finlay contests where reconstruction becomes invention, and Davis replies that the boundary was the book’s question. Both positions are recorded; neither settles the method.
strands.works: The Return of Martin Guerre (1982–83); Finlay and Davis, AHR Forum (1988)

micro.scope_note: Italian microstoria and German Alltagsgeschichte have distinct origins and aims; scale alone is not membership in either project. Evidence, narrative and generalization remain contested within this umbrella. Kracauer is a retrospective comparison, not a claimed founder. González’s Mexican microhistoria is included as a distinct local-history project; shared terminology does not establish transmission from Italian or German programmes.

carlo_ginzburg.label: Carlo Ginzburg
carlo_ginzburg.date_label: The Cheese and the Worms: Italian original (1976) · Miti, emblemi, spie: first Italian collection (1986) · Clues, Myths, and the Historical Method: English translation (1989) · Microhistory: Two or Three Things That I Know about It (1993)
carlo_ginzburg.description: A historian of popular culture and evidentiary inference whose Menocchio study became a central example of Italian microhistory. In his 1993 retrospective he presents microhistory as testing categories through contextual and anomalous cases, without automatically transferring conclusions between scales. He joins awareness that research and narrative are constructed to resistance to skeptical textual reduction. His Clues essay compares interpretation of small traces in art attribution, detection and psychoanalysis. These are his methodological arguments, rather than a definition binding all microhistorians.
carlo_ginzburg.representative_figures_and_works: The Cheese and the Worms (Italian 1976); Miti, emblemi, spie (Italian collection 1986; Clues, Myths, and the Historical Method, English translation 1989, translated by John and Anne C. Tedeschi; selected essay read); “Microhistory: Two or Three Things That I Know about It” (1993, translated by John and Anne C. Tedeschi).
carlo_ginzburg.scope_note: The 1976 book remains unread as a whole; its date and Menocchio context retain the earlier reviewed publisher record. New reading on 2026-10-24: selected Clues pp. 96–101 through the university-hosted scan/OCR; 1993 Microhistory pp. 22–24, 26–30, 32–34 reread. Original Italian, full Clues essay and cited Freud/Morelli works were not collated. The 1986 Italian collection and its 1989 English translation are dated separately from the earlier component essays; the 1989 translation is on the editions track, not an original-contribution milestone. The 1993 retrospective explicitly denies that Kracauer’s work founded his microhistorical practice; retrospective affinity is not transmitted influence. The existing qualified group-endpoint claims about Ginzburg are reattached to this individual entry with their IDs and evidence intact. No life dates, complete career interval or review-through year are asserted.

giovanni_levi.label: Giovanni Levi
giovanni_levi.date_label: I pericoli del geertzismo: Italian original (1985) · Inheriting Power: English translation (1988) · Les usages de la biographie (1989) · Os perigos do geertzismo: Portuguese translation (1999) · Frail Frontiers? (2019)
giovanni_levi.description: A social historian and practitioner of microhistory who studies the room for action within conflicting norms and unequal relations. His essay on biography distinguishes ways that individual lives can illuminate social inquiry without assuming coherent groups or unconstrained actors. In the 1985 Geertzism essay he criticizes fixed cultural contexts and circular interpretation while acknowledging the force of interpretive work. In 2019 he distinguishes microscopic reading from merely small subjects and questions the assumptions joining some broad global histories to microhistory; he does not reject every connected history.
giovanni_levi.representative_figures_and_works: L’eredità immateriale (Italian 1985; Inheriting Power, English translation by Lydia G. Cochrane, 1988; book body unread); “I pericoli del geertzismo” (1985, read in its 1999 Portuguese translation); “Les usages de la biographie” (1989, translated by Olivier Christin); “Frail Frontiers?” (2019, opening read).
giovanni_levi.scope_note: Existing readings and their translation limits remain. Reread on 2026-10-24: complete ten-page Portuguese Geertzism translation (1999), especially pp. 142–146; original Italian uncollated. The earlier complete official OCR reading of the 1989 biography essay is retained, with its opening reread in Persée; OCR quotations were not newly reproduced. Inheriting Power remains known through bibliography and Ginzburg’s named account, not a new whole-book reading. The 2019 contribution is read in the publisher-rendered opening and notes only, after direct access failed; the limited argument about global histories is attributed accordingly. Geertz’s and Darnton’s books were not independently re-read. Older person-specific critiques retain their original edge IDs and qualifications.

quentin_skinner.label: Quentin Skinner
quentin_skinner.date_label: Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas (1969) · The Foundations of Modern Political Thought (1978) · Liberty before Liberalism: inaugural lecture (1997) · Liberty before Liberalism: extended published essay (1998) · On Encountering the Past: interview with Koikkalainen and Syrjämäki (2002)
quentin_skinner.description: A historian of political thought who asks what historically situated writers were doing with their words. His 1969 argument treats public conventions and possible interventions as evidence against reading timeless doctrines out of classic texts. His later first-person account credits Collingwood, Wittgenstein and analytical philosophy while warning against tidy intellectual autobiography. Liberty before Liberalism states a program of recovering a neo-Roman account of civil liberty displaced by liberal predominance. Contextual inquiry is itself contested: Pocock’s 1996 discussion singles out Skinner’s search for the modern state as vulnerable to imposing later categories on earlier actors.
quentin_skinner.representative_figures_and_works: “Meaning and Understanding in the History of Ideas” (1969); The Foundations of Modern Political Thought (1978, unread here; particular criticism mediated by Pocock); Liberty before Liberalism (lecture 12 November 1997; extended book 1998, preface and pp. 1–4 read); “On Encountering the Past” (2002 interview with Petri Koikkalainen and Sami Syrjämäki).
quentin_skinner.scope_note: No complete career review or whole-book reading. Prior source qualifications remain. Fresh 2026-10-24 reading: 1969 article pp. 37–38 and 50–52; 2002 manuscript answers 1 and 6; Liberty before Liberalism preface ix–xiv and printed pp. 1–4, with the publisher copyright leaf distinguishing first publication 1998 from lecture 1997 and Canto reissue 2012; Pocock’s published 1996 criticism at pp. 54–55. The original Collingwood passage remains uncollated. Skinner’s retrospective recollection is explicit reception evidence, not a shared method of every Cambridge historian. Collective edges that also name Dunn, Pocock or Brett stay on the group entry; only claims specifically about Skinner move to his individual endpoint.

j_g_a_pocock.label: J. G. A. Pocock
j_g_a_pocock.date_label: The Ancient Constitution and the Feudal Law (1957) · The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry (1962) · The Machiavellian Moment (1975) · Concepts and Discourses: A Difference in Culture? (1996) · Barbarism and Religion: volumes 1 and 2 (1999) · Barbarism and Religion: volume 6, Barbarism: Triumph in the West (2015) · John Robertson, John Pocock’s Histories of Historiography (2025)
j_g_a_pocock.description: A historian of political thought and historiography who reconstructs the languages in which political thinking becomes possible. His methodological inquiry treats thinking as historical activity rather than only as coherent philosophy. The Machiavellian Moment presents a selective inquiry into republican fragility in time. In the 1996 concepts-and-discourses exchange he welcomes conceptual lexicons but questions whether they can reconstruct the complexity of political languages, and criticizes Skinner’s search for the modern state for risking anachronistic categories. John Robertson’s later account follows the historiographical problem from the ancient constitution to the six volumes of Barbarism and Religion; those books remain mediated rather than newly read here.
j_g_a_pocock.representative_figures_and_works: The Ancient Constitution and the Feudal Law (1957, known through bibliography and John Robertson’s account); “The history of political thought: a methodological inquiry” (1962, selected 2009 reprint); The Machiavellian Moment (1975, introduction read in the retained source review); “Concepts and Discourses: A Difference in Culture?” (1996); Barbarism and Religion (six volumes, 1999–2015; dated and discussed through Robertson, 2025).
j_g_a_pocock.scope_note: Fresh reading 2026-10-24: printed pp. 3–4, 9–11 in the 2009 publisher excerpt of the 1962 methodological inquiry; the complete 1996 concepts-and-discourses contribution pp. 47–58; Robertson’s 2025 article pp. 1–4 closely, with later sections/endnotes consulted for the six-volume sequence. The earlier reading of The Machiavellian Moment introduction vii–x is preserved, not represented as a newly read complete book. No body of the 1957 or 1999–2015 books was read. Pocock explicitly cannot read German and discusses the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe through Richter; the new objections preserve that limit and his praise of complementary inquiry. His private correspondence and late political essays were not read. The 1996 publication is separate from the December 1992 symposium.

reinhart_koselleck.label: Reinhart Koselleck
reinhart_koselleck.date_label: Kritik und Krise (1959) · Preussen zwischen Reform und Revolution (1967) · Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe: first volume, coedited with Brunner and Conze (1972) · Vergangene Zukunft: original collection (1979) · Futures Past: Keith Tribe’s English translation (1985) · A Response to Comments on the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe (1996) · Zeitschichten (2000) · Malin Dahlstrom reviews Olsen’s History in the Plural (2012)
reinhart_koselleck.description: A historian of political and social concepts and of historical time. He distinguishes words from concepts, the language of sources from analytical categories, and semantic change from direct reduction to social structures. He coedited the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe with Otto Brunner and Werner Conze; collective authorship is retained. In Futures Past he examines the relation between experience and expectation, and in his published 1996 response he argues that the unique context of a speech act does not exclude tracing later reuse and transformation of concepts. His reply to Pocock defends the interdependence of conceptual and discourse history. Later accounts of his early books and temporal layers are explicitly mediated through Malin Dahlstrom’s review of Niklas Olsen.
reinhart_koselleck.representative_figures_and_works: Kritik und Krise (1959); Preussen zwischen Reform und Revolution (1967); with Otto Brunner and Werner Conze, Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe (first volume 1972, collective series); Vergangene Zukunft (1979; Keith Tribe’s English Futures Past, 1985; Columbia reissue 2004); “A Response to Comments on the Geschichtliche Grundbegriffe” (1996); Zeitschichten (2000). The 1959, 1967 and 2000 books are known here through Dahlstrom’s account of Olsen, not direct book-body readings.
reinhart_koselleck.scope_note: The retained Futures Past source records the exact earlier selected chapter/preface readings and their limits. Fresh 2026-10-24 reading: chapter 5 pp. 85 and 91–92, with the surrounding analytical distinctions; the 1996 reply pp. 59–66 closely, plus its concluding context; the complete six-page Dahlstrom review of Olsen. Original German texts, lexicon articles and the full 1959/1967/2000 books were not read. The lexicon’s 1972 date is bibliographic metadata; its methodological account rests separately on the primary reply and existing primary passages. Nietzsche’s quotation and Weber’s typology are specific resources, not total genealogies. New prose paraphrases rather than reproduces source quotations. The early-book reception is a reader’s report of another reader, with no new direct claim about Habermas’s uncollated review.
